record.paper_title: Observational Cosmology: caveats and open questions in the standard model
record.original_question: Do the oldest Galactic stars truly have ages of 16–19 billion years or more, exceeding the standard cosmological age estimate of about 13.7 billion years, or are the stellar and cosmological age measurements still too inaccurate to establish a real conflict?

evidence.quote: Controversy also surrounds the age of the Universe. Cosmologists say the Universe is 8 to 15 billion years old, 13.7 Gyr according to the recent measures of WMAP[240], while stellar astronomers claim that the oldest stars in the Galaxy are as high 16 to 19 billion years old[259] or even older.
At present we have no firm proof for the age of the stars larger than the predicted age of the Universe by the standard model.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $t_\star$ denote the age (in years) of the oldest stars in the Milky Way Galaxy, determined from stellar astrophysics (e.g., main-sequence turnoff fitting in globular clusters, white-dwarf cooling sequences, or nucleocosmochronology of metal-poor halo stars). Let $t_U$ denote the age of the Universe (in years), determined from cosmological observations within the standard $\Lambda$CDM framework (e.g., the cosmic microwave background, baryon acoustic oscillations, and Hubble-constant measurements), with a fiducial value near $t_U \approx 1.37 \times 10^{10}$ yr.

Determine which of the following holds:

(a) The oldest Galactic stars genuinely satisfy $t_\star \gtrsim 1.6\text{–}1.9 \times 10^{10}$ yr, so that $t_\star > t_U$ at a statistically significant level, indicating a real tension with the standard cosmological age estimate; or

(b) The current uncertainties in both the stellar age determinations and the cosmological age determination are large enough that the intervals for $t_\star$ and $t_U$ overlap, so that no statistically significant conflict can be established.

In other words, decide whether the inequality $t_\star > t_U$ holds at a meaningful confidence level given the best current observational and modeling uncertainties, or whether the apparent excess of stellar ages over the cosmological age is consistent with measurement and modeling errors.
artifact.status_search_result: Subsequent measurements have effectively resolved the apparent conflict. Early Hipparcos-era estimates giving ages of 16–19 Gyr for the oldest halo stars (e.g., HD 140283) have been revised downward with improved parallaxes (HST, Gaia), updated stellar-evolution models, and better treatment of uncertainties. Current best estimates for the oldest Galactic stars are about 13.8 ± 0.4 Gyr, consistent within errors with the Planck cosmological age of 13.787 ± 0.020 Gyr. The consensus is that the stellar and cosmological ages now agree within uncertainties, so no real conflict is established.

status_evidence.title: HD 140283 - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: A 2013 study used Hubble to estimate the star's age at 14.46±0.8 Gyr; subsequent stellar-evolution models revised the age to ~13.7 or 12 Gyr.
status_evidence.claim: The age estimate of the 'Methuselah' star has been revised downward to be consistent with the age of the Universe.

status_evidence.title: How old is the universe? The oldest stars give us a clue
status_evidence.snippet: Using latest stellar-evolution models, the oldest known star's age is 13.8±0.4 Gyr, consistent with the cosmological age.
status_evidence.claim: Updated stellar ages agree with the Planck cosmological age within uncertainties.

status_evidence.title: Age of the universe - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: Planck 2018 gives the age of the universe as 13.787±0.020 Gyr; stellar ages with proper uncertainties are consistent with this value.
status_evidence.claim: Stellar and cosmological age determinations are now compatible.
